title: Hormone Therapy Slashes Osteoporosis Risk by 69% — and South Asian Women May Have the Most to Gain
excerpt: A new study presented at ENDO 2026 adds to growing evidence that menopausal hormone therapy protects bone density. For South Asian women — who face earlier menopause and higher fracture risk — the findings carry extra urgency.
body:
For decades, many women approaching menopause have been told to steer clear of hormone replacement therapy. The fear — born from a landmark 2002 study that linked HRT to elevated breast cancer risk — kept millions of women from using a treatment that could have eased their symptoms and protected their bones.

Now a growing body of evidence is pushing the medical consensus back toward a more nuanced position. And the latest data, presented Sunday at ENDO 2026, the Endocrine Society's annual meeting in Chicago, may be the strongest signal yet that it's time to reconsider.

The Numbers Are Hard to Ignore

In a retrospective cohort study of 387 postmenopausal women who underwent DEXA bone density scans between 2021 and 2025, those using menopausal hormone therapy had a 69 percent lower risk of low bone mineral density in their spine and hip — the two sites where osteoporotic fractures are most common and most devastating.

The finding held even after researchers controlled for age, time since menopause, vitamin D levels, smoking, and other health conditions.

"This study revisits that narrative and shows that menopausal hormone therapy may have an important added benefit: protecting bone health," said lead researcher Diego Espinoza-Peralta, vice president of the Mexican Society of Nutrition and Endocrinology. "That shifts the conversation from 'avoid if possible' to 'reconsider in the right patient.'"

Among the cohort, 48.1 percent had low bone mineral density. But those on HRT showed significantly higher density at both the lumbar spine and total hip, with the protective association remaining strong and statistically significant across subgroups.

Why This Matters More for South Asian Women

The global data is striking enough. But for women of South Asian descent — whether living in India, the UK, the US, or Canada — the implications are arguably more urgent.

Research from the University of Surrey found that pre-menopausal South Asian women already show elevated bone resorption — the process by which bone tissue is broken down — compared to white Caucasian women of the same age. This elevated breakdown, typically seen only after menopause, suggests South Asian women may be losing bone earlier and faster than their peers.

A separate Indian study of ambulatory postmenopausal women found osteoporosis prevalence as high as 48 percent, with widespread vitamin D deficiency and poor dietary calcium intake compounding the problem. Indian women also tend to reach menopause earlier — the average age is 46 to 47 years, compared to 51 in Western countries — giving bone loss a longer window to accumulate.

For NRI women in their 40s and 50s, this creates a double burden: the genetic and dietary vulnerabilities carried from South Asia, combined with the stress, dietary shifts, and sometimes reduced sun exposure of life abroad.

The Fear That Kept Women Away

The hesitation around HRT traces back to the Women's Health Initiative, a massive US trial that in 2002 reported increased risks of breast cancer, heart disease, and stroke in women taking combined estrogen-progestogen therapy. The headlines were alarming, and HRT prescriptions plummeted almost overnight.

But subsequent reanalysis of the data — and more than two decades of additional research — has substantially softened that picture. The risks were found to be concentrated in older women who started HRT well after menopause, and the absolute risk increases were small. For women starting HRT near menopause onset (the "timing hypothesis"), the cardiovascular risks appear minimal and may even be protective.

A Mendelian randomization study published in the International Journal of Women's Health in 2026 provided genetic evidence supporting HRT's bone benefits, finding that ever-use of hormone therapy was causally associated with higher bone mineral density in women aged 45 to 60.

What NRI Women Should Consider

The ENDO 2026 findings don't mean every menopausal woman should start HRT. The decision remains personal, factoring in individual risk profiles for breast cancer, cardiovascular disease, and blood clotting.

But the evidence increasingly suggests that for many women — particularly those at elevated risk of osteoporosis — the bone-protective benefits of HRT deserve a seat at the table alongside its well-known relief from hot flashes, night sweats, and mood disturbances.

For diaspora women with aging mothers in India, the conversation may be even more direct: the combination of early menopause, poor calcium intake, vitamin D deficiency, and cultural reluctance to discuss menopause openly means many South Asian women are losing bone silently, without screening or intervention.

The ENDO 2026 study's message is simple: menopausal hormone therapy appears to independently protect bones. For a population already at elevated risk, that protection could mean the difference between an active old age and one defined by fractures, disability, and lost independence.
